lessons.title: ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು (dayaviṭṭu) — please (having placed compassion)
lessons.gloss: please (dayaviṭṭu — "having placed compassion," from ದಯ daya "compassion")

needs: your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, because the lesson points at something written down. You can listen to all of it now and come back to the parts that need looking at once you have stopped.

segments.text: Kannada's everyday "please" is, once you open it up, a small act of generosity: "having placed compassion" between us.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: The word

segments.text: ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು (dayaviṭṭu) = please, literally "having placed compassion / kindness." Two pieces:
ದಯ (daya) = compassion, kindness, grace — from Sanskrit daya.
ಇಟ್ಟು (iṭṭu) = "having placed / set down," from the verb ಇಡು (iḍu) "to place, to put."
So dayaviṭṭu means, at heart, setting kindness down (before you) — asking the listener to act from compassion.

That is exactly how Tamil builds it (tayavu seytu, "do the kindness"), and the same instinct as Arabic min faḍlik ("from your grace") and Hindi kṛpayā (from kṛpā, "compassion"). A wide arc of Asia says please by naming the kindness it hopes for.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart: The Dravidian family, side by side

segments.text: daya + a light verb, four times over:
Kannada ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು dayaviṭṭu — compassion + having placed.
Tamil தயவுசெய்து tayavu seytu — kindness + do.
Telugu దయచేసి dayacēsi — compassion + having done.
Malayalam ദയവായി dayavāyi — compassion + as / having become.

blocks.title: Why it's said this way: about how it's used

segments.text: The honest note: a standalone please-word is a little formal / emphatic. Everyday Kannada politeness leans on the respectful command — the verb ending ‑ಿ (-i): ಕುಳಿತುಕೊಳ್ಳಿ (kuḷitukoḷḷi) "please sit," ಹೇಳಿ (hēḷi) "please tell me." That ending already means "please" do this. Add ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು (dayaviṭṭu) in front when you want to underline the courtesy.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: Sound and structure

segments.text: Look at ಟ್ಟು — a doubled ṭ. The first ಟ್ is ṭa silenced by the virama (its vowel cut), and it tucks under the next letter as an ottu (a subscript form) before ಟು ṭu. Kannada writes a double consonant by stacking, not repeating side by side — a neat contrast with how the Roman alphabet just writes "tt."

segments.instruction: the everyday way — the verb ending: "kuḷitukoḷḷi" = please sit
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the everyday way — the verb ending: "kuḷitukoḷḷi" = please sit]

segments.text: What is the Kannada word for please? (ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು dayaviṭṭu.) What do its pieces mean? ("Compassion" daya + "having placed" iṭṭu.) Which cousins ask the same way? (Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam with daya — plus Arabic faḍl, Hindi kṛpā.) What carries "please" in ordinary speech? (The respectful verb ending ‑ಿ -i.)

lessons.title: ◌್ (virama) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ್ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ◌್ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ◌ು — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
◌್ (virama) — no sound of its own — it takes one away.

It is a vowel-killer. Every consonant in this script arrives with an a already inside it — that is what an abugida is. This mark takes the a back, leaving the bare consonant. It is how the script writes two consonants in a row.
You already say these, and every one of them has ◌್ (virama) somewhere inside it:
ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ namaskāra — hello / greetings (namaskāra — "a making of a bow").
ಧನ್ಯವಾದ dhanyavāda — thank you (dhanyavāda — "an utterance of 'worthy'").
ಇಲ್ಲ illa — no / there isn't (illa — the negative).
ನನ್ನ nanna — my.
Put your pen on ◌್ (virama) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

needs: a pen and something to write on

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ಗ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ◌ೆ — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
ಗ — ga.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not g, it is ga.
You already say these, and every one of them has ಗ (ga) somewhere inside it:
ಹೇಗೆ hēge — how.
ನೀವು ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ? nīvu hēgiddīrā — how are you? (respectful).
ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ cennāgi — well, nicely — and the reply "ನಾನು ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದ್ದೇನೆ.
ಪರವಾಗಿಲ್ಲ paravāgilla — it's okay / no problem / you're welcome.
